text:
Apollo 13: The Long Way Home

Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on April 11, 1970, bound for the Fra Mauro highlands of the Moon. It was to be the third lunar landing, and the public had already begun to treat such flights as routine. The commander, Jim Lovell, was on his fourth spaceflight and had orbited the Moon once before, on Apollo 8. Fred Haise would fly the lunar module with him to the surface. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier, after the original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, was exposed to German measles and grounded by the flight surgeons.

For two days the flight went well. On the evening of April 13 the crew gave a television tour of their spacecraft, which the major networks did not bother to carry live. The ship was really two vehicles docked nose to nose. The command module, Odyssey, was the cone-shaped cabin in which the crew would ride home, and it was attached to a cylindrical service module that held the main engine and the oxygen, hydrogen and fuel cells that supplied power, water and air. The lunar module, Aquarius, was a spindly, thin-skinned lander built to carry two men to the Moon's surface and support them for about two days.

A few minutes after the broadcast ended, about 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked Swigert to perform a housekeeping chore: switching on the fans that stirred the super-cold oxygen in the service module's tanks. Seconds later the crew heard a loud bang and felt the ship shudder. Warning lights came on across the instrument panel. "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here," Swigert radioed. Asked to repeat, Lovell came on: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first, controllers in Houston suspected the instruments, because the readings showed so many things failing at once that it seemed impossible. They were real. One of the two oxygen tanks had burst. The blast had damaged the plumbing of the other, which was now leaking. Lovell looked out a window and reported that the spacecraft was venting a gas into space. It was the ship's oxygen, and with it went the fuel cells that needed oxygen to make electricity. Within about three hours, Odyssey would be dead except for the small batteries and oxygen supply reserved for re-entry.

The Moon landing was abandoned almost at once. The question now was whether the crew could be kept alive. Flight director Gene Kranz and his team, followed by a fresh shift under Glynn Lunney, settled on the only real option: use Aquarius as a lifeboat. Haise and Lovell scrambled through the tunnel to power up the lander, a process that normally took hours and that they compressed drastically, while Swigert shut down Odyssey to save its batteries for the end of the trip. Before the command module went dark, they transferred its navigation alignment to the lander's computer by hand, with Lovell asking Houston to check his arithmetic.

The spacecraft was still heading toward the Moon, and turning around directly would have required the main engine in the service module, which no one trusted after the explosion. Instead, the crew would swing around the far side of the Moon and let its gravity sling them back. Apollo 13 had earlier left the "free return" path that would do this automatically, so the crew fired the lander's descent engine to get back onto it. As they passed behind the Moon, some 250 kilometers above the surface they would never walk on, they were farther from Earth than any humans had ever been. Two hours after the closest approach they fired the engine again, for more than four minutes, to shorten the trip home by about ten hours and aim for the Pacific Ocean.

That still left nearly three days of coasting in a vehicle designed for two men and two days, now carrying three men for four. Oxygen was not the problem; the lander had enough. Electricity and water were. The lander's batteries had to be stretched, and its equipment was cooled by water, which meant drinking water competed with the machinery. Nearly everything that could be switched off was. The crew rationed themselves to about six ounces of water a day each, a fraction of what they needed. With the heaters off, the cabin temperature sank to a few degrees above freezing. Condensation beaded on the walls and instrument panels. The men slept badly, in snatches, and Haise developed a kidney infection that left him feverish and shivering.

A more immediate danger was the air itself. Each breath the astronauts exhaled added carbon dioxide to the cabin, and the lander's chemical filters, canisters of lithium hydroxide, were being used up. Odyssey had plenty of spare canisters, but they were square, and the sockets in Aquarius were round. On the ground, engineers gathered the items they knew were aboard and improvised an adapter from plastic bags, the cardboard cover of a flight manual, a spacesuit hose and duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew step by step. The astronauts built the contraption, switched it on, and watched the carbon dioxide level, which had been climbing toward dangerous territory, fall back.

Meanwhile, the ship kept drifting off course, and the crew had to make a correction without their navigation computer, which was shut down to save power. Lovell steered by keeping the Earth centered in his window, lining up crosshairs on the boundary between its day and night sides, while Haise helped hold the ship steady and Swigert timed the fourteen-second burn with his wristwatch. It worked.

In Houston, teams that included the grounded Mattingly worked in the simulators to solve the final problem: how to restart a frozen, damp command module using almost no power. No such procedure existed. They wrote one in a few days, testing each switch setting against the batteries' meager supply, and read it up to Swigert line by line as he copied it down by hand.

On April 17, with Earth filling the windows, the crew moved back into Odyssey. They cast off the service module and saw, for the first time, what had happened to it: an entire side panel had been blown away, leaving a tangle of wreckage exposed. Then they released the lander that had kept them alive. "Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you," Mission Control radioed.

No one knew whether the explosion had cracked the heat shield, or whether the parachutes would work after days in the cold. During re-entry, the hot gases around the capsule blocked radio signals, as expected. But the silence went on well past the time controllers had predicted, for about a minute and a half longer. Then Swigert's voice came through, and television cameras picked up the capsule hanging beneath three parachutes over the South Pacific. Odyssey splashed down near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, just under six days after launch. All three men were exhausted, dehydrated and thinner, and alive.

Investigators later traced the explosion to a chain of small oversights years in the making. The oxygen tank had been jarred in the factory, and thermostat switches inside it were never upgraded for the higher voltage used at the launch site. During a ground test weeks before launch, the tank's heaters ran for hours, the switches welded shut, and the overheated wiring lost its insulation. When Swigert switched on the fans, a spark did the rest.

NASA came to call Apollo 13 a "successful failure": a mission that missed the Moon but brought its crew home.
